name: Ruth Nakamura, ICU: SGLT2-inhibitor-associated DKA with E. coli urosepsis and delirium

caseMeta.title: ICU then medical ward: SGLT2-inhibitor-associated near-euglycemic DKA with E. coli urosepsis and delirium in a 67-year-old with type 1 diabetes: insulin with D10W from the start, potassium 3.3 with the insulin held, sepsis bundle, sulfonamide allergy and culture narrowing, falls, an asymptomatic low (3 days, checkpoints at every 0700 and 1900)
learningObjectives: Recognize near-euglycemic DKA from an SGLT2 inhibitor (glucose 210, bicarbonate 9, gap 24, BHB 6.8, arterial pH 7.12) and apply the adult protocol: insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h with D10W from the start, hourly glucose with a written D10W titration, and the resolution criteria (BHB under 0.6 plus venous pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher); do not stop insulin at a closed gap with ketones still present.

Apply the peripheral potassium rule: hold insulin for K 3.3, replace with KCl 10 mEq/100 mL riders one at a time (never more than 10 mEq/h from all sources, lactated Ringer's counted at 4 mEq/L, potassium-free saline carrier), restart only at K 3.5 or higher with prescriber confirmation, and use the glargine 2-hour overlap before the drip stops.

Run the sepsis bundle and the antibiotic plan: cultures before antibiotics, 30 mL/kg reassessed fluids, lactate trend, ceftriaxone, culture-directed narrowing to amoxicillin, and the sulfonamide-allergy trap (TMP-SMX reported susceptible but contraindicated); recognize the inadequate respiratory compensation (Winter's formula) on the first gas.

Manage delirium and fall risk without sedatives or restraints, recognize an asymptomatic low glucose (hypoglycemia unawareness), and teach euglycemic-DKA recognition, a blood-ketone meter, CGM reconnection, glucagon and the permanent SGLT2-inhibitor stop with the daughter.

problems.name: SGLT2-inhibitor-associated DKA with near-normal glucose (type 1 diabetes, 52 years)
problems.details: Glucose 210, arterial pH 7.12, bicarbonate 9, anion gap 24, BHB 6.8 at 0110. Empagliflozin (started September 24, off-label in type 1 diabetes) permanently discontinued. Insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h = 6 units/h with D10W from the start; hourly POC glucose; potassium and magnesium watched. Resolves only with BHB under 0.6 plus pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher.

problems.name: Sepsis from a probable urinary source (right pyelonephritis)
problems.details: Fever, right flank tenderness, nitrite-positive pyuria, WBC 18.6, lactate 3.2 at 0110. Blood cultures x2 and urine culture before ceftriaxone (0140). Lactated Ringer's 1,800 mL = 30 mL/kg. Ultrasound: no obstruction. Cultures pending.

problems.name: Acute metabolic encephalopathy (infection-associated delirium)
problems.details: Independent cognition before this illness. Inattentive, oriented to person and place, CAM-ICU positive. Assisted mobility, reorientation, family presence; no benzodiazepines or restraints.

problems.name: Acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.2, baseline 0.7)
problems.details: Prerenal from fever, vomiting and glycosuric volume loss. Lisinopril held; no NSAIDs; strict I&O; creatinine reviewed before potassium.

problems.name: Hypokalemia on insulin: K 3.3 at 0650 (potassium chloride riders given in the ED)
problems.details: K 4.8, 4.0, 3.3. Mild T-wave flattening with small U waves on the 0705 ECG. Insulin held; one KCl 10 mEq/100 mL rider at a time (10 mEq/h maximum from all sources); magnesium 1.6 and phosphorus 2.0 watched.

problems.name: Type 1 diabetes for 52 years with hypoglycemia unawareness, mild distal neuropathy and nonproliferative retinopathy
problems.details: Home glargine 18 units at 2100 and lispro with meals (pens; CGM receiver connection lost 2 days before admission). Sometimes no symptoms until glucose is under 50. HbA1c 8.1%.

problems.name: Allergy: sulfonamide antibiotics (generalized urticaria)
problems.details: No penicillin or cephalosporin allergy. Check the allergy list at every antibiotic dose; a culture report may list trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as susceptible: not an option for her.

problems.name: VTE prophylaxis: enoxaparin 40 mg daily (age 67, sepsis, ICU stay with reduced mobility)
problems.details: Risk-model score 4 (reduced mobility 3 + acute infection 1). Platelets 240; estimated creatinine clearance 43 mL/min or higher. Inpatient only.

problems.name: E. coli pyelonephritis: narrowed to oral amoxicillin (7 calendar days)
problems.details: Final urine culture susceptible to ampicillin and ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin resistant, no ESBL. TMP-SMX appears susceptible but is contraindicated by her allergy. Amoxicillin 1,000 mg every 8 hours through 11/11 at 2200. Blood cultures preliminary no growth.

problems.name: Fall risk with an assisted near-fall at 2015 on Day 2
problems.details: Impulsive about toileting; neuropathy and tubing add risk. Hands-on assistance for every transfer, scheduled toileting, walker; physical therapy Day 3. No injury.

problems.name: Asymptomatic hypoglycemia: glucose 63 at 2100 on Day 3
problems.details: No warning symptoms (impaired awareness). Treated with 15 g juice (88 at 2115) and a snack. Glargine reduced to 10 units and lispro ratio to 1 unit per 18 g; no bedtime correction.

orders.name: Full Code (daughter Emi Tanaka is the health-care agent if capacity is lost; capacity reassessed as the delirium improves)

Establish peripheral IV access in the ED and add two more by 0200 (three in all, no central line, no arterial catheter): A insulin alone; B lactated Ringer's and D10W through separately controlled pumps and a pharmacy-verified manifold; C sequential potassium, magnesium and the antibiotic. Assess every site hourly during infusions; remove when no longer needed
orders.instructions: Never flush insulin-containing tubing into the patient and never interrupt the dedicated insulin line for routine flushing: use IV C or B for compatible medicines and line care. Priming volume is discarded before connection and is not counted as intake. Draw laboratory samples from an arm without an infusion running.

orders.name: Continuous cardiac monitoring and strict intake and output with every void measured (assisted clean catch for the first urine, no indwelling catheter); reassess lungs, capillary refill, mentation and fluid responsiveness before each crystalloid bolus
orders.instructions: Sepsis with DKA and acute kidney injury: reassess after each bolus. She is not to walk to the bathroom alone (confusion).

orders.name: ECG 12-lead now (DKA, sepsis, possible potassium disturbance); acquire 0115, interpretation released 0130

Initial labs (ED): BMP, magnesium, phosphorus, beta-hydroxybutyrate, arterial blood gas (single radial puncture), lactate, albumin, CBC, HbA1c at 0110. TWO sets of blood cultures from separate peripheral sites (0112 and 0115) and an assisted clean-catch urinalysis and urine culture (0118), ALL before the first antibiotic dose. Repeat chemistry, arterial gas, BHB, magnesium, phosphorus and lactate at 0320 and again at 0650 (with a CBC); stop serial lactate once it is under 2 and perfusion is improving
orders.instructions: Results are released about 10-20 minutes after collection. Draw from an arm without an infusion running. DKA resolves only when BHB is under 0.6 AND venous pH is 7.3 or higher OR bicarbonate is 18 or higher.

orders.name: insulin regular (HUMULIN R) 100 units in 0.9% sodium chloride 100 mL (1 unit/mL) infusion - DKA (fixed rate)
orders.instructions: Regular insulin 100 units in NS to 100 mL (1 unit/mL) on its own pump channel and IV A, 6 units/h, NO bolus. Independent two-nurse check of drug, concentration and rate at initiation and every change. POC glucose hourly, including any hold. HOLD at once for K under 3.5, suspected severe hypoglycemia or urgent deterioration and notify; keep checking glucose and keep dextrose running. Restart only when K is 3.5 or higher AND the prescriber confirms. Do not stop for a normal glucose or for gap closure alone. Final discontinuation needs the transition order and the glargine overlap.
orders.rationale: 60 kg x 0.1 unit/kg/h = 6 units/h; no bolus. Near-euglycemic DKA (SGLT2 inhibitor): the ketoacidosis, not the glucose of 210, is the target, so D10W runs from the start with the insulin. Insulin is held for K under 3.5. The fixed 0.1 unit/kg/h rate with extra dextrose is used here rather than lowering to 0.05 when glucose is under 250; call the prescriber if glucose cannot be held in range.
nursingConsiderations: Hourly POC glucose; strict I&O; telemetry.
High-alert drug: two-nurse check of drug, concentration, rate and patient.
Stop only by order, after the first subcutaneous basal insulin dose has had its overlap.

medication.importantInfo: The ketones and acid-base balance, not the glucose number, decide when insulin stops. SGLT2 inhibitors keep glucose low (glycosuria) while ketones rise, so the glucose can look reassuring. Insulin moves potassium into cells: the blood level can fall quickly.
medication.freqKey: Continuous (adult DKA protocol)

orders.name: dextrose 10% in water (D10W), 1,000 mL bag, with the insulin infusion
orders.instructions: D10W titration (POC glucose hourly): goal about 150-200. POC 100-149: increase D10W by 50 mL/h and notify the prescriber, recheck in 1 hour (sooner if symptoms). POC 70-99: notify immediately, increase glucose support and recheck in 15 minutes. POC under 70: temporarily hold the insulin infusion, treat with the hypoglycemia order, check every 15 minutes and obtain insulin and dextrose restart orders once safe. POC over 200 on two checks, or if more than 200 mL/h of D10W would be needed: call the prescriber for an individual insulin, dextrose and volume review rather than escalating without limit. Never stop the insulin only because the glucose is normal: the ketones are the target. Impaired hypoglycemia awareness: a normal-looking glucose with no symptoms does not exclude a falling trend. Run on IV B through its own pump (separate from the insulin). Hypotonic: watch the sodium with each panel and the lungs and urine every 2 hours.
orders.rationale: Near-euglycemic DKA: dextrose begins with the insulin so the ketones can be cleared without hypoglycemia. 100 mL/h = 10 g/h; 150 mL/h = 15 g/h.

orders.name: POTASSIUM SAFETY PROTOCOL: three peripheral IVs; never more than 10 mEq/h from ALL sources (lactated Ringer's counts at 4 mEq/L); one KCl 10 mEq/100 mL rider at a time; no 40 mEq/L bags; no potassium in maintenance fluid; HOLD insulin if K is under 3.5; continuous telemetry
orders.instructions: PERIPHERAL POTASSIUM SAFETY PROTOCOL (three peripheral IVs, no central line): before ANY potassium, confirm urine output of at least 0.5 mL/kg/h (30 mL/h at 60 kg) and review the latest creatinine. TOTAL IV potassium from ALL sources on ALL lines must NEVER exceed 10 mEq per hour. Lactated Ringer's counts (it contains 4 mEq/L): never run it alongside a potassium chloride rider; use potassium-free 0.9% sodium chloride as the carrier while a rider runs. No potassium is added to any maintenance fluid. Never IV push; never a 40 mEq/L bag (central-line strength). Riders are premixed KCl 10 mEq in 100 mL over 1 hour on a pump, ONE at a time, never in parallel. K 5.0 or higher = no potassium. K 3.5-4.9 = the prescriber chooses zero to two sequential riders by the trend, renal function and remaining insulin exposure (aim about 4-5). K UNDER 3.5 = HOLD the insulin infusion and notify the prescriber at once; then up to four sequential riders (40 mEq) with a recheck after two and at completion; restart the insulin only when K is 3.5 or higher AND the prescriber confirms. Stop replacement and call urgently for an unexpected result, urine under 30 mL/h, an arrhythmia, extravasation or new pain at the site. Inspect the peripheral site and ask about pain every hour during a rider; do not speed the rate. Telemetry throughout. Draw K from a site away from the infusing lines.
orders.rationale: Adult DKA protocol: K under 3.5 is replaced before and during insulin; peripheral lines limit the rate to 10 mEq/h.

K 3.3 (0650 specimen, released 0700): HOLD the insulin infusion NOW and notify the prescriber. Reduce D10W to 50 mL/h while insulin is held; continue hourly POC glucose. Stop lactated Ringer's and run potassium-free 0.9% sodium chloride at 100 mL/h. Four sequential KCl 10 mEq/100 mL riders at 0700, 0800, 0900 and 1000 on a pump, one at a time. Draw a potassium at 0900 (before the third rider starts). No insulin restart until a repeat K is 3.5 or higher and the prescriber has reviewed it
orders.instructions: Independent check of the new pump settings. Do not accelerate the potassium. Inspect the peripheral site and ask about pain every hour. Persistent DKA (BHB 4.1) despite the low glucose: the hold is for potassium safety, and it is as short as possible.

orders.name: potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL premixed piggyback (unit riders 1-4)
orders.frequency: Four sequential riders, 0700, 0800, 0900 and 1000, one at a time on a pump; 10 mEq/h maximum from all sources
orders.instructions: Peripheral IV C (left antecubital 18 g), pump, ONE bag at a time, never in parallel, never IV push. stickyNotes.title: Potassium: peripheral IVs, 10 mEq/h limit
stickyNotes.body: Three peripheral IVs, no central line. TOTAL potassium from ALL sources on ALL lines never more than 10 mEq per hour, and lactated Ringer's counts (4 mEq/L): use potassium-free saline while a KCl rider runs. No 40 mEq/L bags, no potassium in maintenance fluid. K under 3.5: HOLD insulin, call, then KCl 10 mEq/100 mL over 1 hour ONE bag at a time (up to four), urine at least 30 mL/h, recheck after two. Peaked T = high K; flat T + U waves = low K; a normal tracing does not exclude either.

stickyNotes.title: Insulin and D10W (60 kg)
stickyNotes.body: 6 units/h (0.1 unit/kg/h), no bolus, WITH D10W from the start (near-normal glucose, SGLT2-inhibitor DKA). Goal glucose about 150-200. POC 100-149: raise D10W by 50 mL/h and call; 70-99: call now, recheck in 15 minutes; under 70: hold insulin, treat, check every 15 minutes. Never stop insulin for a normal glucose or a closed gap alone: DKA is over only with BHB under 0.6 AND (pH 7.3 or higher OR bicarbonate 18 or higher). Impaired hypoglycemia awareness: no symptoms does not mean safe.

stickyNotes.title: Allergy: sulfonamide antibiotics
stickyNotes.body: Sulfonamide antibiotics cause generalized urticaria (no anaphylaxis). No penicillin or cephalosporin allergy. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can appear as "susceptible" on a culture report: it is NOT an option for her. Check the allergy list at every antibiotic dose.

stickyNotes.title: Delirium and falls
stickyNotes.body: Confused and inattentive on arrival; worse at night. Assisted mobility and toileting only, bed alarm on, hourly rounding, reorient at every contact, glasses and hearing aids, daytime light, sleep protection, family presence. No benzodiazepines, routine sedatives or restraints. Look for treatable causes (glucose, oxygen, pain, urine retention, infection) when attention worsens.

stickyNotes.title: Empagliflozin stopped permanently
stickyNotes.body: Off-label SGLT2 inhibitor for type 1 diabetes caused this DKA. Do not restart any SGLT2 inhibitor. Lisinopril is on hold (dehydration, AKI). Urine glucose stays strongly positive for days after the last dose, so a urine dipstick glucose is not a useful marker now.

stickyNotes.title: Insulin held for K 3.3
stickyNotes.body: Insulin infusion held at 0700. D10W 50 mL/h and hourly glucose continue. Four KCl 10 mEq/100 mL riders one at a time with potassium-free saline; K at 0900 before the third rider; restart only when K is 3.5 or higher AND the prescriber confirms.

stickyNotes.title: Transition (2300)

notes.title: ED Provider Note - Sepsis Evaluation, Possible DKA
notes.author: T. Quillen, MD
notes.summary: Acute confusion, dysuria, right flank pain and vomiting in a 67-year-old with type 1 diabetes of 52 years on an SGLT2 inhibitor. Dry, deep-breathing, right costovertebral-angle tenderness, inattentive, no focal deficit. Sepsis from a urinary source is likely and DKA is possible despite the home glucose of 198. Samples sent and cultures collected before antibiotics; fluid resuscitation started.
notes.body:
**HPI**
67-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since age 15 (hypoglycemia unawareness, mild distal neuropathy, nonproliferative retinopathy), hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Dysuria and frequency began two days ago; yesterday she had urgency, feverishness, reduced drinking and right flank discomfort; at 1800 she was nauseated and vomited once. Her meter read 198, so she assumed she could not have DKA. Her daughter Emi Tanaka found her confused on the telephone at 0030 and EMS brought her in. She took glargine 18 units at 2100 as usual and lispro 3 units with lunch, and skipped dinner insulin because she did not eat.

**Medicines and allergy**
Glargine 18 units at 2100, lispro 1 unit per 12 g carbohydrate plus 1 unit per 50 mg/dL over 150 with meals, empagliflozin 10 mg at 0800 (started September 24 by an outside prescriber for glucose and weight, off-label in type 1 diabetes), lisinopril 5 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, nasal glucagon as needed. **Allergy: sulfonamide antibiotics (generalized urticaria, no anaphylaxis).** No penicillin or cephalosporin allergy. Personal CGM; the receiver connection was lost two days ago.

**Exam**
Temperature 39.1 C orally, heart rate 118, BP 92/54, respirations 28 and deep, SpO2 97% on room air. Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill about 4 seconds, right costovertebral-angle tenderness, lungs clear, no focal neurological deficit. GCS 14: oriented to person and place, not to date, and inattentive.

**Plan**
Sepsis with probable pyelonephritis and possible DKA. Blood chemistry, magnesium, phosphorus, BHB, arterial gas, lactate, albumin, CBC and HbA1c were collected at 0110; the first blood-culture set is drawn and the second is being obtained, then an assisted clean-catch urine for urinalysis and culture, all before antibiotics. Lactated Ringer's 500 mL boluses with lung and perfusion reassessment between each, ondansetron for nausea, ECG now, strict output collection. Results are pending.

notes.body:
**Measurements**
Ventricular rate 118 bpm. PR 156 ms. QRS 86 ms. QTc 445 ms (Fridericia).

**Interpretation**
Sinus tachycardia. Normal T-wave contour without pathological peaking, no QRS widening, no ischemic ST pattern, no arrhythmia.

**Context**
DKA with sepsis; potassium 4.8 on the first specimen (released 0130). Insulin will move potassium into the cells while the total body potassium is low, so the level is expected to fall: recheck at 0320 and keep her on telemetry.

notes.title: ED Provider Note - Diagnostic Update, DKA and Sepsis
notes.author: T. Quillen, MD
notes.summary: Panel released 0130: glucose 210, bicarbonate 9, gap 24, BHB 6.8, arterial pH 7.12 (pCO2 29), lactate 3.2, creatinine 1.2 (baseline 0.7), WBC 18.6; urine nitrite-positive with pyuria. SGLT2-associated DKA with near-normal glucose, urinary sepsis, delirium and AKI. Ceftriaxone at 0140; insulin without a bolus with D10W from the start.
notes.body:
**Data (released 0130)**
Glucose 210, sodium 134 (corrected for glucose about 135.8), potassium 4.8, chloride 101, bicarbonate 9, anion gap 24, BHB 6.8, BUN 36, creatinine 1.2, magnesium 1.8, phosphorus 3.8, albumin 3.8 (no gap correction needed), lactate 3.2, WBC 18.6, hemoglobin 13.0, platelets 240, HbA1c 8.1%. Arterial gas: pH 7.12, pCO2 29. Urinalysis: nitrite positive, large leukocyte esterase, over 100 WBC per high-power field, many bacteria, glucose 1,000 mg/dL or more and ketones 3+. ECG: sinus tachycardia 118 with normal T waves.

**Assessment**
1. **DKA with near-normal glucose, associated with the SGLT2 inhibitor.** Glucose 210 is just above the strict 200 cut-off for euglycemic DKA, but the acidosis is severe by bicarbonate and moderate by pH; a reassuring glucose must not delay treatment. Empagliflozin is discontinued permanently.
2. **Respiratory compensation is inadequate.** Winter's formula predicts an arterial pCO2 of 21.5 (19.5-23.5); the measured 29 means a superimposed respiratory component. Reassess airway protection, fatigue and aspiration risk now; do not call it simple Kussmaul breathing. A repeat arterial gas follows at 0320.
3. **Sepsis from a urinary source** (pyuria, nitrite, flank tenderness, fever, lactate 3.2) with encephalopathy and acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.2 is 1.7 times her baseline of 0.7, stage 1). Cultures were collected before antibiotics; ceftriaxone 2 g starts at 0140 (no ESBL history; allergy is to sulfonamides only).
4. Acute infection-associated delirium. Aspiration precautions, no sedatives.

**Plan**
Intensive-care admission. Complete 30 mL/kg lactated Ringer's (1,800 mL) by 0300 with reassessment. Regular insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h = 6 units/h with no bolus, started with D10W 100 mL/h so the ketones can clear without hypoglycemia; hourly glucose; potassium surveillance (K 4.8 now, expect a fall). Renal and bladder ultrasound for the urinary source.

notes.title: ED Nursing Treatment Reassessment
notes.author: K. Dunmore, RN
notes.summary: Three lactated Ringer's boluses complete (1,800 mL = 30 mL/kg). Ceftriaxone given 0140 after blood and urine specimens. Insulin and D10W both started 0200 on separate pumps after an independent check; no insulin bolus. POC glucose 0300: 194. Follows simple instructions, inattentive; no vomiting since the antiemetic.
notes.body: Three peripheral IVs are patent (A right forearm 20 gauge for insulin alone, B left forearm 20 gauge for lactated Ringer's and D10W, C left antecubital 18 gauge for ceftriaxone and later potassium). The three crystalloid boluses are complete, a total of 1,800 mL, with lung and perfusion reassessment between each bolus (lungs clear throughout). Ceftriaxone 2 g was given from 0140 after both blood-culture sets and the urine specimen had been collected. Regular insulin began at 0200 at 6 units per hour on its own line after an independent dose and pump check, with D10W at 100 mL per hour started at the same time. The 0300 bedside glucose is 194. Acetaminophen 650 mg was given rectally at 0150 for fever, and ondansetron 4 mg at 0120; she has not vomited again. Ruth remains inattentive but follows simple instructions, and her daughter Emi is at the bedside. Urine is measured with assisted collection and she is not allowed to walk to the bathroom alone.

notes.title: ED Provider Note - Repeat Labs and Potassium Replacement
notes.author: T. Quillen, MD
notes.summary: 0320 panel released 0330: arterial pH 7.25, pCO2 24 (appropriate compensation), bicarbonate 10, gap 21, BHB 5.7, lactate 2.2, potassium 4.0 and falling. Two potassium chloride riders with potassium-free saline; insulin and D10W continue. Renal and bladder ultrasound ordered.
notes.body:
The 0320 specimen was released at 0330. Arterial pH 7.25 and pCO2 24: Winter's expected pCO2 is 23 (21-25), so compensation is now appropriate and the earlier respiratory concern has settled. Bicarbonate 10, anion gap 21, BHB 5.7: improving on insulin but far from resolved. Lactate has fallen from 3.2 to 2.2 after resuscitation (repeat once more with the next panel). Glucose 192, creatinine 1.1.

Potassium has fallen from 4.8 to 4.0 in 2 hours on insulin with good urine output (350 mL since arrival, about 2 mL/kg/h). Replace now: potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL over 1 hour, two sequential riders on a pump, with potassium-free saline replacing lactated Ringer's (LR carries 4 mEq/L) so the combined delivery never exceeds 10 mEq per hour through the peripheral line. Continue insulin 6 units/h with D10W 100 mL/h and hourly glucose. Renal and bladder ultrasound is ordered for the urinary source and the AKI. Transfer panel at 0650.

notes.title: Renal and Bladder Ultrasound
notes.author: Radiology Service (J. Whelan, MD)
notes.summary: No hydronephrosis, no obstructing stone seen, bladder not distended. No drainage procedure indicated.
notes.body:
**Indication**
Sepsis with probable pyelonephritis, right flank tenderness, acute kidney injury.

**Findings**
No hydronephrosis in either kidney. No obstructing stone seen. The bladder is not distended.

**Impression**
No obstruction. No drainage procedure is indicated at this time; repeat imaging only for failure to improve or new deterioration.
notes.impression: No hydronephrosis or obstructing stone; bladder not distended.

notes.title: ED to ICU Handoff (SBAR)
notes.author: K. Dunmore, RN
notes.summary: SBAR for transfer to the ICU: sepsis from a probable urinary source with DKA (insulin 6 units/h with D10W 100 mL/h, lactated Ringer's 100 mL/h). Three peripheral IVs; no central line. ED totals 0100-0700: intake 3,062 mL, output 850 mL (net +2,212 mL), not to be added to the new shift. 0650 panel collected, not yet resulted.
notes.body:
**Situation**
Ruth Nakamura, 67, type 1 diabetes with DKA (glucose 210) and sepsis from a probable urinary source, transferring to the ICU at 0700 on IV insulin, D10W and lactated Ringer's, with continuous telemetry and hourly glucose checks.

**Background**
Two days of urinary symptoms, then nausea and vomiting and confusion; started empagliflozin 10 mg daily in September (off-label for type 1 diabetes). Sulfonamide antibiotic allergy (hives). Blood cultures x2 and urine culture collected before the first ceftriaxone dose (0140). Resuscitation: lactated Ringer's 1,800 mL (30 mL/kg) by 0300, then 100 mL/h; two potassium chloride riders (0330 and 0430) with potassium-free saline during them; lactated Ringer's resumed at 0530. Insulin 6 units/h and D10W 100 mL/h since 0200. Renal and bladder ultrasound (report 0530): no hydronephrosis or obstructing stone. Weight 60.0 kg. ED totals 0100-0700: intake 3,062 mL (IV fluid 2,700, IV medicine 362), output 850 mL (urine 700, emesis 150), net +2,212 mL; the ICU shift starts its own ledger at 0700.

**Assessment**
Last set 0655: temperature 38.0 C, heart rate 104, BP 116/64, respirations 24, SpO2 98% on room air. Oriented to person and place only, inattentive, follows one-step commands, protects her airway; lungs clear. Last POC glucose 168 (0600). The 0650 transfer panel is collected and NOT yet resulted: potassium is unknown to me.

**Recommendation**
Read the 0650 result as soon as it is released and act on the potassium before anything else; keep hourly glucose, the bed alarm on and assisted toileting; no unassisted walking; reorient her and call Emi with updates (agent if capacity is lost).

notes.title: 12-Lead ECG
notes.author: I. Bergstrom, MD
notes.summary: Sinus tachycardia 104, PR 164 ms, QRS 88 ms, QTc 462 ms (Fridericia, U wave excluded). Mild diffuse T-wave flattening with small U waves; no QRS widening or ventricular ectopy (potassium 3.3).
notes.body:
**Measurements**
Ventricular rate 104 bpm. PR 164 ms. QRS 88 ms. QTc 462 ms (Fridericia; the U wave is identified separately and is not included in the QT).

**Interpretation**
Sinus tachycardia. Mild diffuse T-wave flattening with small U waves best seen in V2-V4. No QRS widening, no ventricular ectopy. Compared with 0115: rate slower (118 to 104) and the T waves are lower with new U waves.

**Context**
Potassium 3.3 on the 0650 specimen (released 0700), magnesium 1.6, on an insulin infusion. Do not mistake a U wave for the end of the T wave when measuring the QT. Correct both deficits, hold the insulin until the potassium is safe, and keep her on telemetry.

notes.title: ICU Admission History and Physical
notes.author: H. Calloway, MD
notes.summary: SGLT2-associated DKA with near-normal glucose, sepsis from a probable urinary source, acute metabolic encephalopathy and improving prerenal AKI. 0650 panel: K 3.3 (insulin held, four peripheral KCl riders, K recheck at 0900), bicarbonate 12, gap 17, BHB 4.1, lactate 1.6, Mg 1.6. ECG 0705: flattened T waves with small U waves. Enoxaparin 40 mg daily for documented clot risk (sepsis, ICU stay, reduced mobility, age 67).
notes.body:
**Reason for admission**
Diabetic ketoacidosis with sepsis from a urinary source, in a woman with type 1 diabetes taking an SGLT2 inhibitor.

**HPI**
67-year-old woman, type 1 diabetes for 52 years. Dysuria and frequency for 2 days, then fever, right flank pain, vomiting and confusion. Empagliflozin 10 mg daily had been started on September 24 by an outside prescriber (off-label in type 1 diabetes); her last dose was yesterday morning, and she took her basal insulin. Meter glucose was 198 so she assumed she could not have DKA. ED course: blood cultures x2 and urine culture before ceftriaxone 2 g (0140); lactated Ringer's 1,800 mL (30 mL/kg) by 0300 then 100 mL/h; regular insulin 6 units/h without a bolus with D10W 100 mL/h from 0200; potassium chloride 10 mEq x2 (0330, 0430); ondansetron; acetaminophen 650 mg rectally. Renal ultrasound (0530): no hydronephrosis or obstruction.

**Past history, medicines, allergy, social**
Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prior uncomplicated UTIs, nonproliferative retinopathy and mild distal sensory neuropathy; hypoglycemia unawareness (sometimes no symptoms until glucose is under 50). Baseline creatinine 0.7. No heart failure, coronary disease, dementia, lung or chronic kidney disease. Home: glargine 18 units at 2100, lispro with meals, lisinopril 5 mg, atorvastatin 20 mg, nasal glucagon 3 mg as needed, empagliflozin (now stopped). **Allergy: sulfonamide antibiotics (generalized urticaria).** Widowed retired librarian who lives alone with her cat, Miso; independent before this illness; no tobacco, alcohol or drugs. Daughter Emi Tanaka (health-care agent if capacity is lost) lives 10 minutes away. Full code.

**Exam**
Weak and dry-mouthed, awake and oriented to person and place only, distractible, follows one-step commands, protects her airway; CAM-ICU positive; no focal deficit. Deep respirations, lungs clear. Right costovertebral-angle tenderness. Three peripheral IVs, no central line. Telemetry: sinus tachycardia with mild T-wave flattening and small U waves (ECG 0705).

**Data (0650 panel, released 0700)**
Glucose 168, sodium 137, **potassium 3.3**, chloride 108, bicarbonate 12, anion gap 17, venous pH 7.28, pCO2 26, BHB 4.1, BUN 29, creatinine 1.0, lactate 1.6, magnesium 1.6, phosphorus 2.0, WBC 17.0. POC glucose 168.

**Assessment and plan**
1. **DKA, improving but NOT resolved** (BHB 4.1, bicarbonate 12) despite the modest glucose. Potassium is below 3.5, so the insulin infusion is **held now** and D10W is reduced to 50 mL/h with hourly glucose. Four sequential potassium chloride 10 mEq riders (0700, 0800, 0900, 1000) through a peripheral IV, never above 10 mEq per hour from all sources, with potassium-free saline replacing lactated Ringer's (LR carries 4 mEq/L); potassium rechecked at 0900. Insulin restarts only when K is 3.5 or higher and I have reviewed it.
2. **Hypomagnesemia and low phosphorus.** Magnesium 1.6 will be rechecked at 1100 and replaced if still low (it makes potassium hard to correct); phosphorus 2.0 is monitored, not replaced.
3. **Sepsis, probable right pyelonephritis.** Lactate normalized (1.6) after 30 mL/kg; no pressor need, no oxygen need. Ceftriaxone continues (next dose due at 0140 tomorrow); cultures pending; no obstruction on ultrasound. Reassess lungs and perfusion before any more fluid.
4. **Acute metabolic encephalopathy (delirium).** Treat the causes; assisted mobility, bed alarm, reorientation, family presence, no benzodiazepines or restraints.
5. **AKI, prerenal and improving** (creatinine 1.2 to 1.0; baseline 0.7). Hold lisinopril, no NSAIDs, strict I&O.
6. **VTE prophylaxis: enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily from 0900.** She has documented clot-risk factors: age 67, sepsis (acute infection), an ICU stay with reduced mobility (assisted mobility only, delirium), a risk-model score of 4 (high risk). No bleeding, platelets 240, estimated creatinine clearance above 40 mL/min (no dose change). Inpatient only.
7. **Impaired hypoglycemia awareness** with D10W and insulin running: hourly POC glucose, hypoglycemia orders in place; no symptoms does not mean safe.
8. Empagliflozin permanently stopped (serious adverse drug reaction documented). Endocrinology consulted for transition planning.

notes.title: ICU Note - Potassium 3.7, Insulin Restart
notes.author: H. Calloway, MD
notes.summary: Potassium 3.7 (0900 specimen, released 0910) after 20 mEq. I reviewed it and authorized restarting insulin at 6 units/h at 0915 with D10W back to 100 mL/h; riders 3 and 4 continue. POC glucose 156 (0800) and 154 (0900) during the hold.
notes.body:
The interim potassium drawn at 0900 (before the third rider) was released at 0910 with a value of 3.7 after two riders (20 mEq). That is above the 3.5 threshold and rising, so I reviewed the result and authorized restarting the regular insulin infusion at 6 units per hour (0.1 unit/kg/h) at 0915, with D10W returned to 100 mL per hour. The third and fourth potassium riders continue one at a time, with potassium-free saline as the carrier. During the 2-hour 15-minute hold the bedside glucose stayed at 156 and then 154 on D10W 50 mL/h: SGLT2 inhibitors keep causing glucose loss in the urine for days, which also explains why her glucose has stayed in the 150s.

The ketoacidosis is still active (BHB 4.1 at 0650), so the insulin is needed even though her glucose is modest. Her mentation is unchanged: she follows one-step commands but needs repeated reminders about why she is in hospital. Peripheral sites are without pain or swelling. The next panel is at 1100 (potassium, magnesium, BHB, gas); keep hourly glucose, and keep the D10W titration protocol active.

**Measurements**
Ventricular rate 96 bpm. PR 160 ms. QRS 86 ms. QTc 446 ms (Fridericia).

**Interpretation**
Sinus rhythm. Normal T-wave contour, no distinct U waves, no conduction abnormality, no ectopy. Compared with 0705: rate slower (104 to 96), the flat T waves and U waves have resolved.

**Context**
Potassium 4.0 on the 1100 specimen (released 1110), after 40 mEq of potassium chloride over 4 hours. Magnesium 1.6 is being replaced. Continue telemetry; the potassium will be rechecked with the 1450 panel.

notes.title: Endocrinology Consultation - DKA, Transition and Hypoglycemia Unawareness
notes.author: L. Ostrander, MD
notes.summary: 1100 panel (released 1110): K 4.0, bicarbonate 14, gap 15, BHB 2.8, glucose 172. Ketones still need insulin at 6 units/h with dextrose titrated; magnesium 2 g now (Mg 1.6). Phosphorus 1.8 monitored, not replaced. Empagliflozin stopped permanently. After resolution: conservative basal-bolus plan with a 2-hour overlap.
notes.body:
**Reason**
SGLT2-inhibitor-associated DKA in long-standing type 1 diabetes with hypoglycemia unawareness; guidance on the insulin course, transition and medicine safety.

**Assessment**
The 1100 panel released at 1110 shows potassium 4.0 (after 40 mEq), bicarbonate 14, gap 15, BHB 2.8 and glucose 172. The glucose is not a marker of how much ketoacidosis remains: the ketones are still high, so insulin continues at 6 units per hour with dextrose adjusted to prevent a low. Magnesium is 1.6 and a 2 g infusion starts now. Phosphorus is low at 1.8 but she has no respiratory muscle weakness or other reason to replace it; the threshold is under 1.0 or those signs.

**Recommendations**
1. Continue the fixed-rate infusion with the D10W titration until DKA resolves (BHB under 0.6 AND venous pH 7.3 or higher OR bicarbonate 18 or higher), then give long-acting insulin and keep the infusion on for a full 2 hours.
2. Permanently discontinue empagliflozin and all SGLT2 inhibitors; list the reaction in the allergy and adverse-reaction record. Warn the team that glycosuria and ketosis can persist for several days after the last dose, so urine glucose is not a useful marker.
3. Conservative subcutaneous regimen after resolution: low basal dose and meal insulin by carbohydrate actually eaten, with no bedtime correction. Her age, recent AKI, uncertain intake and impaired awareness argue against restarting her full home doses.
4. Teaching later: euglycemic DKA recognition and a blood-ketone meter, CGM reconnection with a low alert, glucagon, and daughter teach-back.

notes.title: ICU Note - Glucose 148, D10W Increased
notes.author: H. Calloway, MD
notes.summary: POC glucose 148 at 1300 (164 at 1200). D10W increased from 100 to 150 mL/h under the protocol; insulin stays at 6 units/h because BHB 2.8 shows active DKA. She denies symptoms, which does not exclude a decline given her impaired awareness. Mild headache since 1200 without neurological change.
notes.body:
The bedside glucose was 148 at 1300, down from 164 at 1200. She denies symptoms, but her history of impaired hypoglycemia awareness means this does not exclude a clinically important fall. Under the titration protocol (POC 100-149) D10W goes from 100 to 150 mL per hour (15 g of dextrose per hour) and the next check is in one hour. The insulin infusion stays at 6 units per hour because the latest BHB of 2.8 shows ongoing ketoacidosis.

She mentions a mild headache since about noon with no neck stiffness, no focal deficit and no change in her attention; acetaminophen as needed is ordered (the 0150 rectal dose counts toward the daily maximum), and I should be called for any new neurological change. Magnesium 2 g runs 1130-1230. Lungs remain clear and urine output is good, so the added D10W volume is tolerated; sodium is watched with each panel because D10W is free water. Next panel 1450.

notes.title: ICU Note - Gap Closed, Ketones Persist
notes.author: H. Calloway, MD
notes.summary: 1450 panel (released 1500): bicarbonate 17, pH 7.33, gap 11, BHB 1.2, K 3.8, Mg 1.9. The gap has closed but BHB is still 1.2, so DKA is not resolved: insulin and D10W continue. Two more potassium riders at 1500 and 1600.
notes.body:
The 1450 panel released at 1500 shows bicarbonate 17, venous pH 7.33, anion gap 11 and BHB 1.2. The gap has closed and the pH is over 7.3, but the ketoacidosis has not met the resolution criterion because BHB is still above 0.6 and the bicarbonate is under 18. The low bicarbonate with a normal gap reflects a hyperchloremic component (chloride 110) after the saline and lactated Ringer's, not ketones. Stopping insulin now would be premature; insulin 6 units per hour and D10W 150 mL per hour continue.

Potassium has fallen to 3.8 on insulin after 40 mEq earlier, so two more sequential riders (1500 and 1600), one at a time on a pump, are ordered; D10W and insulin contain no potassium, so delivery is exactly 10 mEq per hour; recheck on the 1850 panel. Magnesium is 1.9 after replacement. She is tolerating supervised clear liquids with no further vomiting.

notes.title: Dietitian Initial Assessment
notes.author: N. Vandermeer, RDN
notes.summary: Supervised clear liquids only; ate and drank very little during the illness. Explained that insulin is needed during illness even when appetite is poor. Detailed carbohydrate counting teaching waits until her attention improves; her daughter can help with food.
notes.body:
Ruth remains on insulin with intravenous dextrose and is limited to supervised clear liquids. She reports eating very little during the illness because nausea and urinary symptoms disrupted her usual routine. I explained that insulin is still needed during illness even when appetite is poor, with carbohydrate support adjusted to the clinical situation. Her attention is variable, so detailed carbohydrate-counting education will be repeated after recovery.

Her usual pattern is about three meals daily; as a retired librarian who lives alone she cooks for herself, and her daughter Emi can help provide food during convalescence. A full meal plan and teach-back session (about 45 g carbohydrate per meal) are planned once the diet advances and concentration improves.

notes.title: ICU Night Handoff Note - Ketones Just Above Threshold
notes.author: S. Abrams, MD
notes.summary: 1850 panel (released 1900): bicarbonate 18, pH 7.35, gap 11, K 4.1, BHB 0.7 (not yet under 0.6): insulin and D10W continue. Urine culture preliminary (released 1800): more than 100,000 CFU/mL gram-negative rods, identification pending. Knows the hospital, asks about her cat.
notes.body:
I am taking over from the day team. The 1850 panel released at 1900 shows bicarbonate 18, pH 7.35, anion gap 11, potassium 4.1 and BHB 0.7. The ketone level has not fallen under 0.6, so DKA is not resolved by the current criterion and the insulin infusion (6 units per hour) and D10W (150 mL per hour) continue; the next panel is at 2250. The urine culture preliminary report released at 1800 describes more than 100,000 CFU/mL of gram-negative rods with identification and susceptibilities pending; ceftriaxone continues.

She recognizes the hospital and asks about her cat but cannot give the date reliably. Her daughter has confirmed that Miso is fed and safe at home. Plan: continue hourly glucose and potassium surveillance, fall precautions with assisted toileting, and protect sleep tonight.

notes.title: ICU Night Note - Nocturnal Disorientation
notes.author: S. Abrams, MD
notes.summary: At 2100 she became more disoriented and said she needed to leave to feed the cat. POC glucose 168 at 2100, so a low glucose did not explain it. CAM-ICU positive; no focal change. Reoriented, brief call with her daughter, assisted to the commode. No sedative or restraint.
notes.body:
I was called at 2100 because Ruth became more disoriented and said she must leave to feed her cat. The bedside glucose at 2100 was 168, so hypoglycemia did not account for the behavior. I examined her: she is inattentive and her thinking is disorganized, but she follows a calm request to sit, has no focal neurological change and no breathing distress. CAM-ICU remains positive, which fits infection-associated delirium that worsens in the evening; it is not dementia (independent cognition before this illness).

Contributors checked: glucose normal, no oxygen need, no retention (she voids with assistance), infection under treatment, no new sedating medicine. Plan: reorient, reduce stimulation, assisted commode, a brief reassuring telephone call with her daughter, lights low and sleep protection after the 2250 panel. No benzodiazepine, antipsychotic or restraint is ordered; I will be called for agitation that is unsafe or any focal sign.

notes.title: ICU Night Note - DKA Resolved, Transition Orders
notes.author: S. Abrams, MD
notes.summary: 2250 panel (released 2300): BHB 0.4, pH 7.36, bicarbonate 19, gap 10, K 4.0: DKA resolved by the ketone and acid-base criteria. Glargine 12 units ordered for 2300; insulin and D10W continue until 0100 for a full 2-hour overlap. Consistent-carbohydrate diet; meal lispro by carbohydrate eaten, no bedtime correction.
notes.body:
The 2250 panel released at 2300 shows BHB 0.4, venous pH 7.36, bicarbonate 19, anion gap 10 and potassium 4.0. DKA is now biochemically resolved by the current criteria (BHB under 0.6 with a pH of 7.3 or higher and a bicarbonate of 18 or higher). Glargine 12 units is ordered for 2300, and both the insulin infusion and the D10W are to continue until 0100 for a full 2-hour overlap; they stop only after the glargine dose is verified, she is drinking and eating, and she has not vomited again.

She is taking supervised fluids without recurrent vomiting, and a consistent-carbohydrate diet is ordered for the transition. Meal lispro will be based on the carbohydrate actually eaten, with no bedtime correction. Delirium and impaired hypoglycemia awareness justify a conservative initial subcutaneous dose (about 0.35 unit/kg per day in total, 21 units, of which basal is 12) and continued supervision. Do not judge the dose from the high infusion rate.

notes.title: ICU Night Note - Transition Orders Carried Out
notes.author: S. Abrams, MD
notes.summary: Glargine 12 units at 2300 verified, 2-hour overlap completed; insulin and D10W stopped at 0100 with POC glucose 178. Tolerating fluids and a small snack. One-hour post-transition glucose due at 0200. Blood cultures: no growth at about 24 hours (preliminary, released 0120).
notes.body:
I reviewed the medication record: the 2300 glargine dose and the 2-hour overlap were verified before the insulin infusion and D10W were stopped at 0100. The bedside glucose at discontinuation was 178. She tolerated oral fluids and a small snack without nausea or vomiting. A one-hour post-transition glucose is ordered for 0200 before routine before-meal and bedtime checks begin; the second ceftriaxone dose is due at 0140.

The first preliminary blood-culture update was released at 0120: no growth at approximately 24 hours. She remains intermittently unsure of the date but accepts reorientation and assisted toileting. Plan: bed alarm and hourly rounding continue; one IV (the antibiotic line) is kept as a lock for hypoglycemia rescue access; chemistry at 0650.

notes.title: ICU Note - Morning Recovery
notes.author: H. Calloway, MD
notes.summary: 0650 panel (released 0700): bicarbonate 21, gap 10, BHB 0.3, creatinine 0.8, WBC 12.8, K 4.0: no recurrent ketosis after the transition. Oriented to person, place and date with better attention; CAM-ICU negative this morning. Blood cultures no growth at about 24 hours. Urine culture still preliminary gram-negative rods.
notes.body:
The morning results released at 0700 show bicarbonate 21, anion gap 10, BHB 0.3, potassium 4.0, creatinine 0.8 and WBC 12.8. There is no biochemical evidence of recurrent DKA after the transition (venous pH 7.38, glucose 164). Ruth is oriented to person, place and date with improved attention, and her CAM-ICU assessment is negative this morning, although she still tires easily and her strength is reduced.

Blood cultures were reported as no growth at approximately 24 hours when the preliminary update was released at 0120. The urine culture remains a preliminary gram-negative rod result, so ceftriaxone continues until identification and susceptibilities return. Assisted mobilization with a walker, meal-based insulin with observed intake, a consistent-carbohydrate diet and multidisciplinary discharge preparation start today (infectious disease, pharmacy, case management, physical therapy and the diabetes educator are ordered). Atorvastatin restarts tonight; lisinopril stays on hold.

notes.title: Infectious Disease Consultation - E. coli Pyelonephritis, Oral Narrowing
notes.author: O. Fenwick, MD
notes.summary: Urine E. coli identified (released 0800); final susceptibilities released 1045: susceptible to ampicillin (MIC 2) and ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin resistant, no ESBL. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole reads susceptible but is contraindicated by her sulfonamide allergy. Ceftriaxone stopped; amoxicillin 1,000 mg every 8 hours from 1400, 7 calendar days total, last dose 11/11 at 2200.
notes.body:
**Assessment**
Febrile complicated urinary tract infection (right pyelonephritis) with sepsis, without demonstrated bacteremia and without obstructed drainage. Urine identification (E. coli) was released at 0800 and the final susceptibility report became available at 1045. The isolate is susceptible to ampicillin (MIC 2 mcg/mL), amoxicillin-clavulanate, ceftriaxone, cefazolin and cefepime, with no ESBL phenotype, and resistant to ciprofloxacin.

**Allergy check**
The laboratory also lists trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as susceptible. She has a documented sulfonamide-antibiotic allergy (generalized urticaria), so that agent is NOT an option; she has no penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, so amoxicillin is safe. A fluoroquinolone is not an option (resistance) and would also add delirium and tendon risk at her age.

**Recommendation**
She is clinically improving, tolerating oral intake, her creatinine has returned to 0.8 and the ultrasound showed no obstruction. I ordered ceftriaxone discontinued (the second dose was given at 0140) and amoxicillin 1,000 mg orally every 8 hours at 0600, 1400 and 2200 starting at 1400. The planned course is seven calendar treatment days including the initial IV therapy, with the last dose on November 11 at 2200 if recovery continues. Final blood-culture results still require follow-up after discharge, and recurrent symptoms, new fever or failure to improve would prompt reassessment of source control and duration.

notes.title: Pharmacy Medication Reconciliation and Safety Review
notes.author: R. Medina, PharmD
notes.summary: Verified the final E. coli susceptibilities, the amoxicillin dose and no penicillin allergy; flagged that the "susceptible" TMP-SMX result must not be used (sulfonamide antibiotic allergy). Empagliflozin flagged as a serious adverse reaction and not to be reconciled back; lisinopril held. Enoxaparin dose appropriate.
notes.body:
I verified the final susceptibility report, the amoxicillin dose (1,000 mg every 8 hours; estimated creatinine clearance by Cockcroft-Gault about 65 mL/min at 60 kg and a creatinine of 0.8, so no renal adjustment) and the absence of a penicillin allergy. The first oral dose remains scheduled for 1400 and the next ceftriaxone dose has been removed from the record. The laboratory lists trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as susceptible; because of her documented sulfonamide-antibiotic allergy a pharmacy alert is placed so it cannot be ordered for her.

Empagliflozin is flagged as a serious adverse drug reaction (SGLT2-inhibitor-associated DKA in type 1 diabetes) and must not reappear on discharge reconciliation; communicate this to the outside prescriber. Lisinopril remains held while kidney function and blood pressure are reviewed. Enoxaparin 40 mg daily is appropriate for her weight and kidney function; platelets are 230 and will be rechecked with each CBC. Glargine is due at 2300 and meal lispro is given after observed intake with no bedtime correction. The patient and her daughter will receive one printed medication list that separates the permanent stop (empagliflozin) from the temporary hold (lisinopril).

notes.title: Case Management - Initial Discharge Assessment
notes.author: C. Easterly, RN CCM
notes.summary: Lives alone and managed her own medicines and meals; daughter Emi lives nearby and will help with the cat and supervision. Insulin and strips are affordable; a blood-ketone meter and strips, replacement CGM supplies and nasal glucagon still need to be verified. Immediate return to fully unsupervised living is not appropriate.
notes.body:
Ruth lives alone in a one-story home with two entrance steps and a railing and normally manages her own medicines, meals and household tasks. Her daughter Emi lives 10 minutes away, has her permission to receive updates, and has agreed to care for the cat, Miso, and provide temporary supervision. The family reports that insulin pens and glucose test strips are affordable through her current coverage.

A blood-ketone meter and strips, replacement CGM supplies and an unexpired nasal glucagon device still need verification before she leaves. Her recent delirium and reduced mobility make an immediate return to completely unsupervised living inappropriate. I am coordinating the physical therapy evaluation, the diabetes educator visit with her daughter, home nursing and follow-up appointments before recommending a final disposition.

notes.body:
**Measurements**
Ventricular rate 80 bpm. PR 166 ms. QRS 86 ms. QTc 438 ms (Fridericia).

**Interpretation**
Sinus rhythm. Normal T-wave amplitude and contour; the U waves seen on Day 1 are gone; narrow QRS; no ectopy. Compared with the Day 1 0705 tracing: rate 104 to 80 and the low-potassium pattern has resolved.

**Context**
Potassium 4.0 on the latest panel (released 1900) with no potassium given since Day 1 and normal intake. Telemetry can continue while she remains in the ICU.

notes.title: ICU Night Note - Evening Update
notes.author: S. Abrams, MD
notes.summary: 1850 chemistry (released 1900): bicarbonate 23, gap 10, K 4.0, glucose 192. Eating her meals; before-dinner glucose 204 adds 1 correction unit to the carbohydrate dose. No rash or stomach upset reported since the first oral antibiotic dose. Oriented in conversation but tends to stand before asking for help.
notes.body:
The evening chemistry released at 1900 shows bicarbonate 23, anion gap 10, potassium 4.0 and serum glucose 192. Ruth has eaten her meals today; the pre-dinner glucose was 204, so the dinner dose is the carbohydrate dose (1 unit per 15 g eaten) plus 1 unit for the correction scale. She has had no rash or gastrointestinal upset since her first amoxicillin dose at 1400, which is reassuring given her sulfonamide allergy (a different drug class).

She is oriented during conversation but tends to stand before asking for assistance. A follow-up ECG is done at 1900 to confirm that the low-potassium changes have resolved. Call-light plan, a walker and a commode are in the assisted-care routine; bedside glucose at 2100 and glargine at 2300 without a bedtime correction dose.

notes.title: ICU Night Note - Assisted Near-Fall Assessment
notes.author: S. Abrams, MD
notes.summary: At 2015 she tried to walk to the bathroom alone, her knees began to buckle and the nurse supported her into a chair: no floor descent, head strike or impact. I examined her: no injury, no focal neurological change. POC glucose 186 at 2015. Hands-on assistance and scheduled toileting reinforced.
notes.body:
I was notified of an assisted near-fall at 2015. Ruth attempted to walk to the bathroom before staff could help; her knees began to buckle and the nurse supported her into a nearby chair, so there was no fall to the floor, no head strike and no other impact. She denies pain. On my examination there is no tenderness over the hips, spine or head, full range of movement in all limbs, no new focal neurological finding and attention at her recent baseline. An immediate bedside glucose at 2015 was 186, which excludes hypoglycemia as the cause.

Likely contributors: deconditioning after 2 days of acute illness, distal sensory neuropathy in both feet, tubing and an unfamiliar room, and impulsivity from resolving delirium. No injury imaging is indicated without a fall, head strike or injury sign. I reviewed the event with Ruth, reinforced hands-on assistance for every transfer and set a scheduled toileting plan. The 2100 glucose and a recheck of neurological status are due; I will be called for any new symptom, pain or change in attention.

notes.title: ICU Note - Ready for Ward Care
notes.author: H. Calloway, MD
notes.summary: 0650 panel (released 0700): bicarbonate 24, gap 9, creatinine 0.8, WBC 9.8. Blood cultures no growth at about 48 hours (released 0120). Fully oriented, recalls the near-fall and agrees to ask for help. DKA and AKI resolved. Transfer to the medical ward ordered for 1000.
notes.body:
The morning panel released at 0700 shows bicarbonate 24, anion gap 9, potassium 4.1, creatinine 0.8 and WBC 9.8. Blood cultures were again reported as no growth at approximately 48 hours when the update was released at 0120. Ruth is fully oriented today, recalls the assisted near-fall, and agrees to ask for help with walking. She is tolerating oral amoxicillin and meals without recurrent urinary pain or vomiting.

DKA and the acute kidney injury have resolved; deconditioning and impaired hypoglycemia awareness remain the discharge concerns. Transfer to the medical ward is ordered for 1000 with continued before-meal and bedtime glucose testing, fall precautions, and planned therapy and family education. Enoxaparin continues while she remains hospitalized.

notes.title: Physical Therapy - Mobility Evaluation
notes.author: E. Whitlock, PT, DPT
notes.summary: Mild bilateral leg weakness and reduced foot sensation. Transfers with a walker and standby assistance after reminders to pause before standing; practiced two entrance steps with a railing and hands-on help, no loss of balance. Recommend a rolling walker, temporary family supervision and home therapy rather than unsupervised mobility.
notes.body:
Ruth demonstrates mild bilateral lower-extremity weakness and reduced distal sensation in both feet. She transfers with a walker and one-person standby assistance after reminders to pause before standing. During a supervised short hallway walk she initially advances the walker too far but corrects the technique with cueing. She practiced two entrance steps using a railing with hands-on assistance and no loss of balance.

I recommend a rolling walker, temporary family supervision and home therapy rather than unsupervised mobility immediately after discharge. Nursing should continue assisted toileting and reinforce the same transfer sequence consistently: pause, feet flat, push up, then grip the walker before stepping.

notes.title: Diabetes Education - Ketones, CGM and Hypoglycemia Rescue
notes.author: M. Brightwell, RN, CDCES
notes.summary: Ruth and her daughter Emi (with her consent) practiced blood-ketone testing and explained that nausea, vomiting, deep breathing or confusion need ketones checked even when glucose is near normal. CGM receiver reconnected with a low alert of 90; hospital dosing still uses bedside testing. They understand empagliflozin is permanently stopped.
notes.body:
Ruth and Emi participated in teaching with Ruth's consent after her transfer to the ward. They correctly explained that nausea, vomiting, deep breathing and confusion require a ketone check even when the glucose is near the usual range, and that her glucose of about 200 hid a serious acidosis this time. Ruth demonstrated blood-ketone testing and explained why basal insulin must continue during illness unless a clinician gives a specific alternative plan. Escalation levels for the discharge plan: a blood ketone of 0.6 to 1.4 means calling the diabetes team now and repeating in 2 hours; 1.5 or higher with vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, new confusion or trouble breathing, or any value of 3 or higher, means the emergency department, not home care.

Emi practiced the insulin pen safety check and reviewed how meal doses depend on the carbohydrate actually eaten. We reconnected the CGM receiver and set a low alert of 90 with sharing to Emi, and reinforced that hospital dosing uses bedside testing. Because Ruth may not feel a low glucose, they reviewed the rescue steps: 15 g of fast carbohydrate and a recheck in 15 minutes, nasal glucagon from Emi if she cannot swallow, and no driving until the hypoglycemia risk and her thinking have been reviewed. Both understand that empagliflozin and any similar SGLT2-inhibitor medicine have been permanently discontinued, and that recurrent symptoms need urgent clinical advice rather than waiting for a very high glucose reading.

notes.title: Dietitian Meal Planning Follow-Up
notes.author: N. Vandermeer, RDN
notes.summary: Ruth can now follow the whole discussion and counted the carbohydrate in a sample meal accurately. Plan: about 45 g carbohydrate per meal; smaller meals allowed with the matching insulin dose; Emi will prepare meals at first. Treat a low with rapid carbohydrate first, then a snack if the next meal is not soon.
notes.body:
Ruth is now able to sustain attention throughout the discussion and accurately counts the carbohydrate in the sample meal. The usual plan is approximately 45 g of carbohydrate at each meal, with the option to eat a smaller amount and receive the corresponding prescribed insulin dose. She and Emi described several easy meals and agreed that Emi will prepare food during the first days at home.

We reviewed maintaining fluids and a source of carbohydrate during illness and contacting the diabetes team early when intake declines. I reinforced that treating a low glucose requires rapid carbohydrate first, with a follow-up snack when the next meal is not soon. Emi will keep a written food and insulin record temporarily so the outpatient team can adjust doses to her recovery and appetite.

notes.title: Case Management - Family Support and Supplies
notes.author: C. Easterly, RN CCM
notes.summary: Emi will stay with Ruth continuously for the first 72 hours after discharge and visit daily afterward; the cat is cared for. Walker, meter, CGM supplies, blood-ketone meter and strips, and nasal glucagon are available for home. Home nursing visit accepted for the day after discharge; endocrinology contact within 48 hours and visits within one week. Discharge still depends on the medical team.
notes.body:
Emi confirms that she will stay with Ruth continuously for the first 72 hours after discharge and continue daily visits afterward. The cat is being cared for, and this concern is no longer prompting Ruth to try to leave unexpectedly. A rolling walker, a functioning glucose meter, CGM supplies, a blood-ketone meter and strips, and an unexpired nasal glucagon device are available for home use.

Home nursing has accepted a visit for the day after the anticipated discharge. Follow-up arrangements include an endocrinology contact within 48 hours and an office visit within one week, with a primary-care review within one week of the temporary lisinopril hold and a basic metabolic panel. Discharge remains dependent on the medical team's reassessment, the final teaching verification and safe glucose control overnight.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Evening Note
notes.author: D. Sandoval, MD
notes.summary: Evening chemistry (released 1900): bicarbonate 24, gap 9, K 4.0, glucose 118. Oriented and conversational with no recurrence of delirium today. Dinner about 30 g carbohydrate (smaller than lunch). Walking more with assistance; continues to deny warning symptoms when asked about past lows. Bedtime glucose due at 2100; glargine 12 units due at 2300.
notes.body:
I am covering the ward overnight. The evening chemistry released at 1900 shows bicarbonate 24, anion gap 9, potassium 4.0 and serum glucose 118. Ruth is oriented and converses appropriately, with no recurrence of delirium during the day. Her dinner was smaller than her lunch (about 30 g of carbohydrate), so the after-meal lispro is calculated from what she actually ate, 2 units at 1 unit per 15 g.

She spent more time walking with assistance today and continues to deny warning symptoms when she discusses past low glucose episodes, which is characteristic of her hypoglycemia unawareness. The bedtime glucose is scheduled for 2100 and glargine 12 units is ordered for 2300. I reviewed the hypoglycemia order set, the need to observe actual intake and the daughter's planned supervision.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Night Note - Asymptomatic Low Glucose
notes.author: D. Sandoval, MD
notes.summary: Routine 2100 glucose 63 with no sweating, tremor, palpitations or hunger. Awake and swallowing safely: 120 mL juice (15 g) under the hypoglycemia order; I was notified at 2105. Recheck 88 at 2115, then a cracker snack; 107 at 2130. No bedtime correction insulin. Endocrinology asked to review the 2300 basal dose.
notes.body:
The routine 2100 bedside glucose was 63 even though Ruth denied sweating, tremor, palpitations or hunger: an asymptomatic low in a woman with known hypoglycemia unawareness. She stayed alert and swallowed safely, so she received 120 mL of juice containing 15 g of rapid carbohydrate under the hypoglycemia order, and I was notified at 2105. At 2115 the repeat glucose was 88, and I ordered the follow-up cracker snack because the next meal is not soon. No bedtime correction insulin has been given.

The nurse remained with her during the immediate recovery. The glucose at 2130 was 107 and the next check is at 2200. Because glargine 12 units is scheduled for 2300 and this low came after a day of improving insulin sensitivity, more walking and a small dinner, I have asked endocrinology for a dose review before 2300; basal insulin is not simply omitted in type 1 diabetes. Her daughter will be updated by phone in the morning.

notes.title: Endocrinology - Insulin Reassessment After Low Glucose
notes.author: L. Ostrander, MD
notes.summary: Reviewed the asymptomatic glucose of 63 and the recovery: 88 at 2115, 107 at 2130. No bedtime correction was given. At 2145 I reduced glargine from 12 to 10 units (first dose 2300) and changed meal lispro to 1 unit per 18 g carbohydrate with the same premeal correction. Basal continues; more monitoring, not omission.
notes.body:
I reviewed the asymptomatic glucose of 63 and the treatment response of 88 at 2115 and 107 at 2130. The episode occurred without a bedtime correction and in the setting of improving insulin sensitivity after resolution of the infection, increased activity and a variable appetite. Because she does not feel lows, her glucose targets should sit slightly higher for now; avoiding all lows for several weeks can partly restore warning symptoms.

At 2145 I reduced the scheduled glargine from 12 to 10 units and changed future meal dosing to 1 unit per 18 g of carbohydrate eaten, keeping the cautious premeal correction scale. Basal insulin will still be given because she has type 1 diabetes, with additional monitoring rather than omission. A further bedside check is planned at 2200 before the revised 2300 basal dose, and a targeted check at 0300. Ruth and her daughter need repeat teach-back of the revised doses and the impaired-awareness rescue plan before discharge.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Morning Note - Discharge Readiness
notes.author: V. Halloran, MD
notes.summary: 0650 panel (released 0700): bicarbonate 24, gap 9, K 4.1, creatinine 0.8, WBC 8.2, Hb 11.8 (mild dilutional fall, no bleeding); POC glucose 145. After the low: 126 at 2200, glargine 10 units at 2300, 132 at 0300. Oriented and able to teach back. Blood cultures no growth at about 72 hours (released 0120); final result pending. Conditional discharge order written for about 1000.
notes.body:
The closing laboratory panel released at 0700 shows bicarbonate 24, anion gap 9, creatinine 0.8, potassium 4.1 and WBC 8.2, with a hemoglobin of 11.8 and platelets of 228 (a mild dilutional fall without bleeding) and a bedside glucose of 145. After the evening low, her glucose reached 126 at 2200, glargine 10 units was due at 2300, and the targeted 0300 glucose was 132. Ruth is fully oriented and can describe the purpose of ketone testing and the permanent empagliflozin discontinuation.

Blood cultures remain preliminary with no growth at approximately 72 hours (released at 0120), and our inpatient team retains responsibility for reviewing the five-day result. I have written a conditional discharge order for an anticipated 1000 departure after breakfast tolerance, her daughter's arrival, supply verification and repeat teaching of the revised insulin regimen (glargine 10 units at 2300, lispro 1 unit per 18 g carbohydrate eaten plus the premeal correction, no bedtime correction). The decision to leave depends on those checks and on no further low glucose; if intake is poor, confusion returns or supervision cannot be arranged, we reassess rather than discharge. Enoxaparin ends at actual discharge.
